questions.q: Let the length of a latus rectum of an ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ be 10 . If its eccentricity is the minimum value of the function $f(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{t}^2+\mathrm{t}+\frac{11}{12}$, $\mathrm{t} \in \mathbf{R}$, then $\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2$ is equal to :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Length of LR $=\frac{2 b^2}{a}=10 \Rightarrow 5 \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{b}^2$...(1)
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{t}^2+\mathrm{t}+\frac{11}{12} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{df}(\mathrm{t})}{\mathrm{dt}}=2 \mathrm{t}+1=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=\frac{-1}{2} \\ & \text { Min value of } \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t})=\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)+\frac{11}{12} \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \frac{-1}{2}+\frac{11}{12}=\frac{3-6+11}{12}=\frac{8}{12}=\frac{2}{3}=\mathrm{e} \\ & \mathrm{e}^2=\frac{1-\mathrm{b}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2} \Rightarrow \frac{4}{9}=\frac{1-\mathrm{b}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}\end{aligned}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}=\frac{1-4}{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{5}{\mathrm{a}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{b}^2=\frac{5 \mathrm{a}^2}{\mathrm{a}}$...(2)
$\begin{aligned} & \text { From (1) \& (2) } \\ & 5 \mathrm{a}=\frac{5 \mathrm{a}^2}{\mathrm{a}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=9, \quad \mathrm{~b}=\sqrt{45}=3 \sqrt{5} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{a} 2+\mathrm{b} 2=81+45=126\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The line $y = x + 1$~meets the ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{4} + \dfrac{y2}{2} = 1$~at two points $P$ and $Q$. If~$r$ is the radius of the circle with $PQ$~as diameter then \left(3r\right)2$ \text{ and } is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Plotting the diagram of given data we have,

Let& $P$~be the point~ \left(- 1 + \dfrac{p}{2}, \dfrac{p}{2}\right)$

Since it lies on the ellipse~$\dfrac{x2}{4} + \dfrac{y2}{2} = 1$, we get~

$\dfrac{\left(- 1 + \dfrac{p}{2}\right)2}{4} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{p}{2}\right)2}{2} = 1 ⇒ \dfrac{3p^{2}}{8} - \dfrac{p}{2\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{3}{4} = 0$

Here~\left({p}_{1} - {p}_{2}\right)2 = \left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)2 - 4\left(- 2\right) = \dfrac{8}{9} + 8 = \dfrac{80}{9}$

We know,~\left({p}_{1} - {p}_{2}\right)2 = PQ^{2}$

$⇒ PQ^{2} = \dfrac{80}{9}$

Now~$r = \dfrac{PQ}{2} ⇒ 9r^{2} = 9\dfrac{\left(PQ\right)2}{4} = \dfrac{9}{4} \times \dfrac{80}{9} = 20$

$

questions.q: Let& $P\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{7}, \dfrac{6}{7}\right), Q, R$~and~$S$~be four points on the~ellipse~$9x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 36$.~Let $PQ$ and $RS$ be mutually perpendicular and pass through the origin. If~$\dfrac{1}{\left(PQ\right)2} + \dfrac{1}{\left(RS\right)2} = \dfrac{p}{q},$~where $p$~and $q$ are coprime, then $p + q$& is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$P\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{7}, \dfrac{6}{7}\right), Q, R$~and~$S$~be four points on the~ellipse~$\dfrac{x2}{4} + \dfrac{y2}{9} = 1$

Now,~$OP = {r}_{1} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{7}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{6}{7}\right)2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{48}{7}}$~where~$O$~is origin,

Let~$P$~be~ \left({r}_{1}cos\theta, {r}_{1}sin\theta\right)$

$P$~lies on ellipse, so we get,

$\dfrac{{r1}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{4} + \dfrac{{r1}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{9} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta}{4} + \dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{9} = \dfrac{7}{48} . . . \left(i\right)$

Let~$R$~be~\left(- {{r}_{2}sin\theta, {{r}_{2}cos\theta\right)~as~$PQ \text{ and } RS$~are perpendicular and pass through origin,

So,~$\dfrac{{r2}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{4} + \dfrac{{r2}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{9} =1$

$⇒ \dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{4} + \dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta}{9} = \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}2} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now adding~equation~ \left(i\right) \text{ and } \left($ii\right)$~we get,

\dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}2} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{7}{48} = \dfrac{31}{144}

Now solving,

\dfrac{1}{PQ^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{RS^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{1}{OP^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{OR^{2}}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{PQ^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{RS^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{1}{{r}_{1}2} + \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}2}\right)

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{PQ^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{RS^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{7}{48} + \dfrac{31}{144}\right) = \dfrac{13}{144} = \dfrac{p}{m}

$∴ p + m = 157$

$

questions.q: The locus of mid-points of the line segments joining  \left(- 3, - 5\right)$~and the points on the ellipse $\dfrac{x2}{4} + \dfrac{y2}{9} = 1$& is :$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Parametric point on the given ellipse is& \left(2sin\theta, 3cos\theta\right)$

Let,~the mid-point of line segments joining \left(- 3, - 5\right)$ and \left(2sin\theta, 3cos\theta\right)$~is~ \left(h, k\right)$

Then, by using mid-point formula, we get

$\dfrac{2sin\theta - 3}{2} = h, \dfrac{3cos\theta - 5}{2} = k$

$⇒ 2sin\theta = 2h + 3, 3cos\theta = 2k + 5$

$⇒ sin\theta = \dfrac{2h + 3}{2}, cos\theta = \dfrac{2k + 5}{3}$

We know,~$\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{2h + 3}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{2k + 5}{3}\right)2 = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4}\left[4h^{2} + 9 + 12h\right] + \dfrac{1}{9}\left[4k^{2} + 25 + 20k\right] = 1$

$⇒ 36h^{2} + 16k^{2} + 108h + 80k + 145 = 0$

Hence, the locus of~ \left(x, y\right)$~is~$36x^{2} + 16y^{2} + 108x + 80y + 145 = 0$

$

$⇒ {E}_{k}: \dfrac{x2}{\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right)2} + \dfrac{y2}{\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right)2} = 1$

Now equation of the chord joining~the points~\left(\dfrac{1}{k}, 0\right) \text{ and } \left($0, $\dfrac{1}{k}\right)~will be,

${L}_{k}: x\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right) +$y\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right) =$1$

$⇒ $\sqrt{k}$x + ky - 1 = 0$

Now ${r}_{k} =$ Perpendicular distance of ${L}_{k}$ from $( 0, 0 )$~we get,

${r}_{k} = \left|\dfrac{- 1}{k + k^{2}}\right|

$⇒ {r}_k^{2} = $\dfrac{1}{k + k^{2}}

Now putting the value of~${rk}^{2}$~in~$\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{20}1{r}_k^{2}$~we get,

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{20}1{r}_k^{2} = \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{20}k + k^{2} = $\dfrac{20 \times 21}{2} + \dfrac{20 \times 21 \times 41}{6}

$= 210 + 2870= 3080$

questions.q: A ray of light through  \left(2, 1\right)$~is reflected at a point $P$ on the $y -$ axis and then passes through the point~\left(5, 3\right) .$~If this reflected ray is the directrix of an ellipse with eccentricity $\dfrac{1}{3}$ and the distance of the nearer focus from this directrix is $\dfrac{8}{53},& then the equation of the other directrix can be:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The reflected point of& \left(2, 1\right)$~is~\left(- 2, 1\right) .$

Equation of reflected ray

$y - 1 = \dfrac{3 - 1}{5 + 2} \left(x + 2\right)$

$⇒ y - 1 = $\dfrac{2}{7} \left(x + 2\right)$

$⇒ 7y - 7 = 2x + 4$

$⇒ 2x - 7y + 11 = 0$

Let the equation of other directrix is

$2x - 7y + \lambda = 0$

Distance of directrix from focus

\dfrac{a}{e} -$ae = $\dfrac{8}{53}, where~$e$~is the eccentricity

$⇒ 3a - $\dfrac{a}{3} = \dfrac{8}{53}~or~$a = $\dfrac{3}{53}

Distance from other focus~\dfrac{a}{e} +$ae$

$= 3a + $\dfrac{a}{3} = \dfrac{10a}{3} = \dfrac{10}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{53} = \dfrac{10}{53}

Distance between two directrix~$= $\dfrac{2a}{e}

$= 2 \times 3 \times $\dfrac{3}{53} = \dfrac{18}{53}

So,~\left|$\dfrac{\lambda - 11}{53}\right| = \dfrac{18}{53}

$⇒ \lambda - 11 = 18$~or~$- 18$

$⇒ 2x - 7y - 7 = 0$~or~$2x - 7y + 29 = 0$

$

Given equation of ellipse and circle are $\dfrac{x2}{9} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{4} = 1$ and $x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$.

$⇒ P ≡ \left($3cos$\theta,$2sin$\theta\right)\text{and}$Q ≡ \left($3cos$\theta,$3sin$\theta\right)

Let, $R ≡ \left(h, k\right)$

$⇒ h = 3cos\theta, k = \dfrac{18}{7}sin\theta$

$⇒ \dfrac{h}{3} = cos\theta, \dfrac{7k}{18} = sin\theta$

So, locus of $R$ is given by, $\dfrac{x2}{9} + \dfrac{49y^{2}}{324} = 1$.

$⇒ e = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{324}{49 \times 9}}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{117}{21}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{13}{7}

$

questions.q: A line passing through the point $\mathrm{P}(\sqrt{5}, \sqrt{5})$ intersects the ellipse $\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{36}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{25}=1$ at $A$ and $B$ such that $(P A) .(P B)$ is maximum. Then $5  \left(P A²+P B²\right) is equal to :$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given ellipse is $\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{y^2}{25}=1$

Any point on line $A B$ can be assumed as
$\mathrm{Q}(\sqrt{5}+\mathrm{r} \cos \theta, \sqrt{5}+\mathrm{r} \sin \theta)$
Putting this in equation of ellipse, we get
$25(\sqrt{5}+r \cos \theta)^2+36(\sqrt{5}+r \sin \theta)^2=900$
Simplifying, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{r}^2\left(25 \cos ^2 \theta+36 \sin ^2 \theta\right)+2 \sqrt{5} \mathrm{r}(25 \cos \theta+36 \sin \theta)-595=0 \\ & \quad|\mathrm{r}|=\mathrm{PA}, \mathrm{~PB}
\end{aligned}$
$\text { Thus, } \begin{aligned}
\text { PA } \cdot \mathrm{PB} & =\frac{595}{25 \cos ^2 \theta+36 \sin ^2 \theta}=\frac{595}{25+11 \sin ^2 \theta} \\ & =\text { maximum, if } \sin ^2 \theta=0
\end{aligned}$
This means line $A B$ must be parallel to $x$-axis
$\Rightarrow y_A=y_B=\sqrt{5}$
Putting $\mathrm{y}=\sqrt{5}$ in equation of ellipse, we get
$\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{1}{5}=1 \Rightarrow x^2=36 \cdot \frac{4}{5}$
Hence,
$\mathrm{PA}^2+\mathrm{PB}^2=\left(\sqrt{5}-\frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{5}+\frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2$
$\begin{aligned} & =2\left(5+\frac{144}{5}\right)=\frac{338}{5} \\ & 5\left(\mathrm{PA}^2+\mathrm{PB}^2\right)=338\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $A ( \alpha, 0 )$ and $B ( 0, \beta )$ be the points on the line $5x + 7y = 50$. Let the point $P$ divide the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $7: 3$. Let $3x - 25 = 0$ be a directrix of the ellipse $E: \dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$ and the corresponding focus be $S$. If from $S$, the perpendicular on the $x -$axis passes through $P$, then the length of the latus rectum of $E$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: $A ( \alpha, 0 )$ and $B ( 0, \beta )$ lies on the line $5x + 7y = 50$.

$⇒ 5\left(\alpha\right) + 7\left(0\right) = 50, 5\left(0\right) + 7\left(\beta\right) = 50$

$⇒ \alpha = 10, \beta = \dfrac{50}{7}$

Also, $P$ divide the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $7: 3$.

$⇒ P ≡ \left(\dfrac{7 \times 0 + 3 \times 10}{7 + 3}, \dfrac{7 \times \dfrac{50}{7} + 3 \times 0}{7 + 3}\right)

$⇒ P ≡ \left(3, 5\right)$

$⇒ ae = 3$ as perpendicular from $S$ passes through $P$

Now, $3x - 25 = 0$ is a directrix of the ellipse $E: \dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{25}{3}$

We know that, directrix of an ellipse is given by $x = \pm \dfrac{a}{e}$

$⇒ \dfrac{a}{e} = \dfrac{25}{3}$

Also, $ae = 3$

$⇒ a = 5, b = 4$

Length of LR $= \dfrac{2b^{2}}{a} = \dfrac{32}{5}$

$

Now, finding $Z$ we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y - 3}{1} = - \dfrac{\left(4 + 3\right) - 6}{4 + 1}$

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y - 3}{1} = \dfrac{- 1}{5}$

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{- 1}{5}, \dfrac{y - 3}{1} = \dfrac{- 1}{5}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{12}{5}, y = \dfrac{16}{5}$

$⇒ Z ≡ \left(\dfrac{12}{5}, \dfrac{16}{5}\right)

Eccentricity of ellipse is given as \dfrac{1}{2}.

Now, finding $b^{2}$ using eccentricity formula we get,

$⇒ b^{2} = a^{2}\left($1 - e^{2}\right) = $\dfrac{a2}{2}

So, equation of ellipse will be,

$⇒ $\dfrac{144}{25a^{2}} + \dfrac{256}{25 \times \dfrac{a2}{2}} =$1$ {as \left(x, y\right) ≡ \left(\dfrac{12}{5}, \dfrac{16}{5}\right) }

$⇒ $\dfrac{144}{25a^{2}} + \dfrac{512}{25a^{2}} =$1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{656}{25a^{2}} =$1$

$⇒ a^{2} = $\dfrac{656}{25}

$⇒ b^{2} = $\dfrac{328}{25}

Length of latus rectum is given by,
$L = $\dfrac{2b^{2}}{a}.

$⇒ L = $\dfrac{2 \times \dfrac{328}{25}}{\dfrac{656}{5}}

$⇒ L = $\dfrac{656}{5}

$⇒ L^{2} = $\dfrac{656}{25}

questions.q: If the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse $x^{2} + 4y^{2} + 2x + 8y - \lambda = 0$~is $4$, and $l$ is the length of its major axis, then $\lambda + l$& is equal to _____.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,&

$x^{2} + 4y^{2} + 2x + 8y - \lambda = 0$~is a ellipse

Now on rearranging the terms we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(x + 1\right)2}{\lambda + 5} + \dfrac{\left(y + 1\right)2}{\lambda + 54} = 1$

We know that length of latus rectum is~$\dfrac{2b^{2}}{a} = 4$~

So,~$\dfrac{2\left(\lambda + 5\right)}{4\left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right)} = 4$

$⇒ \dfrac{2 \left(\lambda +$5\right)}{4} = 4 \left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right)

$⇒ \left(\lambda +$5\right) = 8 \left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right)

$⇒ \left(\lambda +$5\right)2 = 64 \left(\lambda +$5\right)$

$⇒ {λ}^{2} + 25 + 10\lambda = 64 \left(\lambda +$5\right)$

$⇒ {λ}^{2} - 54\lambda - 295 = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = 59$\text{or} -$5$

But~$\lambda \ne - 5$

So,~$l = 2a = 2$\sqrt{\lambda + 5} =$2$\sqrt{64} =$16$

$⇒ \lambda + l = 59 + 16 = 75$

$

questions.q:
Let
$S = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}: 9\left(x - 3\right)2 + 16\left(y - 4\right)2 \le 144\right\}$
and~$T = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}: \left(x - 7\right)2 + \left($y - 4\right)2 ≤ 36\right\}$
The n\left($S ∩ T\right)$& is equal to ______.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$S: 9 ( x - 3{)}^{2} + 16\left(y - 4\right)2 \le 144\text{where}\left(x, y\right)\inN \times N$

On rearranging we get,

$S: \dfrac{( x - 3{)}^{2}}{16} + \dfrac{\left(y - 4\right)2}{9} \le 1\text{where}x, y \in \left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots \ldots\right\}$

Now~$T: \left(x - 7\right)2 + \left(y - 4\right)2 \le 36\text{where}x, y \in R$

Now let~$x - 3 = X: y - 4 = Y$

So, new equation and domain will become,

$S: \dfrac{X2}{16} + \dfrac{Y2}{9} \le 1; X \in \left\{- 2, - 1, 0, 1, \ldots \ldots\right\}$

$T: \left(X - 4\right)2 + Y^{2} \le 36; Y \in \left\{- 3, - 2, - 1, 0, \ldots \ldots\right\}$

Now on plotting the diagram we get,

Now number of point in~$n \left(S ∩ T\right)$~will be given by,

Take~$Y = - 3, - 2, - 1, 0, 1, 2, 3$~and check for~$X$

So, possible for~$S ∩ T$~will be,

When~$Y = 0\left(-2, 0\right), \left(-1, 0\right), \ldots \ldots \left(4, 0\right) \to 7\text{possible case}$

When~$Y = 1$~

\left(-1, 1\right), \left(0, 1\right), \ldots \ldots . \left(3, 1\right) \to 5\text{possible case}$

When~$Y = - 1$~

\left(-1, - 1\right), \left(0, - 1\right), \ldots \ldots . \left(3, - 1\right) \to 5\text{possible case}$

When~$Y = 2$~

\left(-1, 2\right), \left(0, 2\right), \left(1, 2\right), \left(2, 2\right) \to 4\text{possible case}$

When~$Y = - 2$

\left(-1, - 2\right), \left(0, - 2\right), \left(1, - 2\right), \left(2, - 2\right) \to 4\text{possible case}$

When~$Y = 3 & - 3$

\left(0, 3\$right)\left($0, - 3\right) \to $\ttext{Total}2\text{possible case}$

So, total cases will be~$7 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 27$

$

questions.q: If the points of intersection of two distinct conics $x^{2} + y^{2} = 4b$ and $\dfrac{x2}{16} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$ lie on the curve $y^{2} = 3x^{2}$, then $3\sqrt{3}$ times the area of the rectangle formed by the intersection points is _______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given conics are $x^{2} + y^{2} = 4b\text{and}\dfrac{x2}{16} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$.

The intersection point of these conics lie on $y^{2} = 3x^{2}$.

So, putting $y^{2} = 3x^{2}$ in both the conics.

$⇒ x^{2} + 3x^{2} = 4b, \dfrac{x2}{16} + \dfrac{3x^{2}}{b2} = 1$

$⇒ x^{2} = b, \dfrac{b}{16} + \dfrac{3b}{b2} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{b}{16} + \dfrac{3}{b} = 1$

$⇒ b^{2} + 48 = 16b$

$⇒ b^{2} - 16b + 48 = 0$

$⇒ b^{2} - 12b - 4b + 48 = 0$

$⇒ \left(b - 4\right) \left($b - 12\right)$

$⇒ b = 4, 12$ ( $b = 4$is rejected because curves coincide)

$⇒ b = 12$

$⇒ x = $\pm \sqrt{12}

$⇒ 12 + y^{2} = 48$

$⇒ y = \pm6$

Hence points of intersection are $( $\pm \sqrt{12}, \pm$6 )$.

So, length and breadth of rectangle are 2\sqrt{12}\text{and}$12$.

So, the area of rectangle is given by, $A = $2\sqrt{12} \times$12 = $48\sqrt{3}

$⇒ $3\sqrt{3}$A = $48\sqrt{3} \tttimes3\sqrt{3}

$⇒ $3\sqrt{3}$A = 432$

$

questions.q: Let $\mathrm{E}_1: \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$ be an ellipse. Ellipses $\mathrm{E}_1$ 's are constructed such that their centres and eccentricities are same as that of $E_1$, and the length of minor axis of $E_i$ is the length of major axis of $E_{i+1}(i \geq 1)$. If $A_i$ is the area of the ellipse $E_i$, then $\frac{5}{\pi}  \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}A_i\right), is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_1=\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4} \Rightarrow \mathrm{e}=\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ & \mathrm{E}_2: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4}=1 \\ & \mathrm{e}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}=\sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{9}=1-\frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4} \\ & \mathrm{a}^2=\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_2: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4}=1 \\ & \mathrm{E}_3: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1 \\ & \mathrm{e}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}=\sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}} \Rightarrow b^2=\frac{64}{81}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_3=\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\frac{64}{81}}=1 \\ & \mathrm{~A}_1=\pi \times 3 \times 2 \Rightarrow 6 \pi \\ & \mathrm{~A}_2=\pi \times \frac{4}{3} \times 2=\frac{8 \pi}{3} \\ & \mathrm{~A}_3=\pi \times \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{8}{9}=\frac{32 \pi}{81} \\ & \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}}=6 \pi+\frac{8 \pi}{3}+\frac{32 \pi}{81}+\ldots . \infty \Rightarrow \frac{6 \pi}{1-\frac{4}{9}} \Rightarrow \frac{54 \pi}{5} \\ & \therefore \frac{5}{\pi} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{\pi} \times \frac{54 \pi}{5}=54\end{aligned}$
